new_statements.quote: It is generally accepted that in present-day Mixtec varieties, there are at least three underlying tone levels, L, M, and H (McKendry 2013:157). For the purposes of this analysis, which largely relies on the comparison of surface pitch levels, I adhere to this general understanding. [...] Table 9: Tone patterns [YUC column: Pattern 1 *L > LL ('two' ùβì); Pattern 2 *Lˀ > LM/MM ('four' kùmī); Pattern 3 *M > MM ('house' βēʔē); Pattern 4 *Mˀ > MH ('corn'); Pattern 5 *ML > ML ('flower' ītà); Pattern 6 *LM > LM/ML ('adobe' ⁿdòʔō)] There are less common patterns in the varieties surveyed, such as MH or H, which do not show up in these common patterns but do appear in words elicited in the General Wordlist. [...] looking at the realization of the Pattern 2 pattern in YUC, while the most common pattern is LM, there are several words in the group with MM tones, such as 'tortilla' [īʃtā] and 'plate' [kōō]. For Pattern 6, several words in YUC have a LM pattern (see 'adobe' above), while others have ML [...] Most of the varieties share tone patterns most of the time, with the exception of YUC which only shares the same pattern as the other varieties for Pattern 1 and Pattern 3.

new_statements.relation_note: Tone only: three surface levels L/M/H adopted; Table 9 YUC reflexes of six Proto-Mixtec tone patterns; YUC tonally the most divergent of the seven surveyed varieties; L vs M distinguished acoustically; tone-marked YUC wordlists in the appendices. Stress/accent: nothing (terms absent).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Yucunicoco Mixtec is treated as a three-level tone language (L, M, H surface levels transcribed per mora on the bimoraic couplet); first-hand Tone Wordlist gives YUC couplet patterns LL, LM/MM, MM, MH, ML, LM/ML as reflexes of Proto-Mixtec *L, *Lˀ, *M, *Mˀ, *ML, *LM, with rarer MH/H patterns elsewhere in the lexicon; no contour or 'semi-low' patterns reported for YUC (those only in the comparison varieties COI/SJM); floating tones not assessed. Nothing whatsoever is said about stress/accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none (no stress statement of any kind in the work)
new_statements.exceptions: Within-pattern variation in YUC: Proto *Lˀ words mostly LM but some MM ('tortilla', 'plate'); Proto *LM words split LM ~ ML ('grasshopper' [tīkà], 'green bean'); loanword group excluded; author cautions that transcriptions are surface pitches by a non-native fieldworker, checked in Praat (section 5 limitations, pp. 90-91).
new_statements.identity_note: OUR-BIBLIOGRAPHY WORK (held, read, tagged 'read: silent on stress'; Glottolog Glottolog's most extensive description for yucu1254), added: a first-hand TONE statement for this languoid that was never staged (existing_statements is empty). YUC = Yucunicoco in the abbreviation list (p. xi); data recorded by the author in Santa Maria Yucunicoco (General Wordlist + Tone Wordlist), i.e. exactly yucu1254, alongside six Juxtlahuaca-Mixtec [vmc] towns. Silent on stress remains true: 'stress' and 'accent' occur 0 times in the text ('prominence' only inside the McKendry 2013 title in the references).

sources.note: Silent: the words 'stress'/'accent'/'prominence' do not occur in the body. Contains first-hand General Wordlist and Tone Wordlist data recorded in Yucunicoco (YUC) plus six vmc towns, isogloss and tone-pattern analyses (ch. 3), a pitch note distinguishing L from M tone (p.41), and an appendix note (p.115) that underlying CV words lengthen to CVV/CVʔV to satisfy a two-mora minimal word (citing McKendry 2013). Recommends YUC stay under INALI 'mixteco del oeste alto', separate from the other six varieties.
